Vuelta a España 2026: Our sprint form guide

While Tadej Pogačar soaks up all the GC talk ahead of the Vuelta a España, which starts on Saturday in Monaco, the sprinting field is taking shape.

To be honest, said sprinting field at this Vuelta isn’t too deep. I guess the majority of the WorldTour’s fast men saw the parcours and quickly realised that only around four stages would realistically end in a bunch gallop. That said, a green jersey is still up for grabs. That prize has been won by a sprinter each year since 2020, when it was last swept up by a GC contender rather than one of the fast men.

We’ve saved you some time trawling through the start list and found the seven best sprinters coming to the 2026 Vuelta a España. We’ll go through each rider’s record for the year, distilling their form down into a Racing Post-style guide, including their win rate, average stage wins per race and season sprint results.

Jordi Meeus (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe)

Jordi Meeus is one of the few sprinters at this Vuelta to have won a Grand Tour stage before. That said, the Champs-Elysées victory he claimed in surprise circumstances at the Tour de France is now over three years ago.

Meeus has picked up some form in 2026, with four wins under his belt so far. All of those wins came on the second-division against relatively weak competition, however. At WorldTour races, his form hasn’t been quite as convincing, with just two top tens to write home about in stage races.

While form isn’t quite on his side, this is likely to be Meeus’s final Grand Tour for Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, as he is expected to move to Soudal Quick-Step next year.

Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike)

Matthew Brennan has blown hot and cold this season, which is quite the contrast from the dazzling 2025 when he managed to topple every big sprinter in the peloton.

This year, he showed flashes of that form at Kuurne-Brussels-Kuurne, but he faded away after that. He was off the mark at the Tour de Suisse and the Boucles de la Mayenne, despite some weak opposition. His recent performances at the Vuelta a Burgos are more convincing, however. He picked up two stage wins there, but again the opposition was weak.

The Vuelta should reward Brennan’s skills, although he’s set to share the spotlight at Visma with Wout van Aert. The two have worked together in the Classics, but they’ll need to have clear-cut roles in order to succeed here.

Kaden Groves (Alpecin-Premier Tech)

Kaden Groves has been out of action for most of the season. However, Alpecin-Premier Tech have decided to roll the dice and field their Aussie sprinter to one last Grand Tour before he ups sticks and leaves the team at the end of the season.

Groves’ first injury setback of the year saw him suffer from a knee injury that forced him out of action in the spring. Then on his return, he crashed out of the Giro during a hectic finale on Stage 1. He made his comeback at the ADAC Classics a week ago, but a 100th place doesn’t fill me with confidence coming into this Vuelta.

On the other hand, Groves is a dab hand at the Vuelta. He’s won seven stages in Spain, and he’s never left this race without a victory under his belt. Plus, he’s a two-time green jersey winner.

With the pressure on for Groves to secure a big contract for 2027, he’ll be hoping for big things here.

Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike)

Wout van Aert returns to Grand Tour racing after having to avoid the Tour de France due to health problems.

That decision came after a successful spring marked by a string of strong Monument results, including that memorable Paris-Roubaix victory. Since then, he took some time out before returning to winning ways in a bunch sprint at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes. The decision to miss the Tour came shortly after, but Van Aert dominated the Tour of Denmark upon his return in August. There, he performed well in the sprints, showing he might be back to his best ahead of this Vuelta.

This will be Wout’s second appearance at the race. On his previous appearance in 2024, he animated the race to bag three stages, spend a few days in red before moving into the green jersey. A crash in the final week forced him out, but at the time Van Aert looked set to win both green and the polka-dots. Having left the race in unfortunate circumstances, he surely has some unfinished business at this race.

What’s more, for every win he bags at the Vuelta, Van Aert will add 2GB of data to every SIM card in his new WVA mobile network.

Mads Pedersen (Lidl-Trek)

It feels like a distant memory when Mads Pedersen’s 2026 palmarès was hanging on by a thread. Now he’s managed to pick up a Tour stage win and a hard-fought green jersey to round out his collection of Grand Tour points classification prizes.

That takes Pedersen on a streak of three Grand Tours with the points classification. If we overlook his early race DNF at the 2024 Tour, the Dane hasn’t left a Grand Tour winless since 2021.

The Dane has the chance to pick up another green jersey here too. He’s one of the most consistent finishers in the bunch, and he’s been improving his climbing over the past year. A stage win feels like a certainty.

Orluis Aular (Movistar)

Orluis Aular has come very close to a Grand Tour stage win over the past two seasons. At the Giro, he was runner-up on Stage 4, and at the 2025 Vuelta, he finished on the podium on three occasions.

The Movistar sprinter’s 2026 results have been a mixed bag. He’s rarely stood out from the crowd, apart from a couple of top tens at the Giro d’Italia. That said, his best performances seem to often come in three-week races. 

The Venezuelan is a versatile sprinter, so the Vuelta’s lumpier days should suit him. He’s not quite had that edge to take a big win yet, but the weakened sprinting field at this year’s Vuelta should give him some confidence.

Ben Turner (Netcompany Ineos)

This time last year, Ben Turner was in great form. He came off a successful summer and launched into the Vuelta with enough power to win Stage 4 ahead of Jasper Philipsen and Mads Pedersen.

The Brit has had mixed fortunes this year, however. Despite an underwhelming Classics campaign, Turner made the top ten a few times at the Giro d’Italia. A runners-up spot at the recent Czech Tour demonstrates some flashes of form before his final Grand Tour for Ineos before leaving for Quick-Step.

Turner prefers a tough finale, the kind of thing that usually favours Mads Pedersen. Netcompany Ineos will be hungry for a stage win, and have brought Axel Laurence to cover for Turner and add extra firepower in the sprints.
